claims.text: Sudden or severe weakness or breathing symptoms: forced vital capacity and maximal inspiratory force; < 15 mL/kg or < 20 cm H2O means higher risk of ventilatory failure.
claims.quote: If sudden or severe true general weakness or any respiratory symptoms are present, forced vital capacity and maximal inspiratory force must be tested to assess risk of acute ventilatory failure. Patients with vital capacity < 15 mL/kg or inspiratory force < 20 cm H2O are at increased risk.

claims.text: Routine labs unless the cause is obvious: CBC, electrolytes with calcium and magnesium, glucose, kidney and liver tests, TSH, ESR, hepatitis C serology.
claims.quote: Unless the cause is obvious, routine laboratory tests (CBC, electrolytes [including calcium and magnesium], glucose, kidney and liver function tests, TSH, ESR, hepatitis C serologic testing) are usually done.

claims.text: Brain upper motor neuron signs: MRI (CT if MRI is not possible).
claims.quote: If brain upper motor neuron dysfunction is suspected, the key test is MRI. CT is used when MRI testing is not possible
If myelopathy is suspected, MRI can detect lesions in the spinal cord.

claims.text: Neuropathy, myopathy or neuromuscular junction disorder: electromyography and nerve conduction studies.
claims.quote: If polyneuropathies, myopathies, or neuromuscular junction disorders are suspected, the key tests that help differentiate these mechanisms of weakness are electrodiagnostic testing (electromyography and nerve conduction studies).

claims.text: Carpal tunnel: clinical (Tinel, Phalen); nerve conduction testing if severe or uncertain.
claims.quote: If symptoms are severe or the diagnosis is uncertain, nerve conduction testing should be done on the affected arm

claims.text: Head trauma: noncontrast head CT; an epidural hematoma is a lens-shaped hyperdensity that does not cross sutures.
claims.quote: Classic lentiform (lens)-shaped hyperdensity that does not extend across suture lines.
